doc.title: John Abercrombie interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

chapter: Johnny Hammond, Dreams and moving to New York
title: Pay with Hammond and playing Harlem clubs
summary: Pay was $90 in town and $110 on the road; he moved to New York, lived in hotels and played Harlem and New Jersey clubs.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Can you recall what kind of money you were making, in that six nights a week thing?
Well I do know that after I played with him for like a year it was, I think the deal was it was $90 a week in town, I remember him telling that once, and then $110 on the road, pay your own hotel.
Let me do the math there.

Yeah. Well everything was so much cheaper in those days, and we used to stay at hotels that were pretty much near the clubs, a lot of them were in ghettos so they weren’t so expensive. And it didn’t really cost that much money to be on the road in those days. But I remember him telling me that, $90 a week in town, $110 on the road, pay your own hotel. So if I worked with him, when I moved to New York, that was when I moved to New York. I don’t know what he paid me in Boston, it was probably less, because I was just a student. And then I went kind of on the road with him and we played — I moved to New York and I used to live in a hotel. In those days you could get a hotel by the week and it would be like twenty-some bucks a week, with maid service. So I’d live in these hotels and we’d play a lot of times at Count Basie’s Lounge, or these clubs in Harlem. It was Count Basie’s, there was a club called Wells, it was near Small’s Paradise, which I never played at, but there was about three or four of them, Club Baron, which I did play

at. There was a place in New Jersey called the Key Club that I played at. And so you’d start to play all these joints and then, that’s when he started paying me a little more money. And I began to become more of a professional musician. I also was out of Boston and now I was in New York. And I didn’t stay there, I went back to Boston, and it took me a couple of times to actually land in New York. Even when I met Mike and Randy I was still torn between Boston and New York. But I went on the road with this band called Dreams. Now I was in a completely different thing. With Johnny I wore a suit and tie and I played “If I Were a Bell” and blues, and all these kind of tunes. And when I started playing with the Dreams band I wore leather pants and headbands and I played with wah- wah pedals and played over one chord. I mean I got a real identity crisis. I didn’t know where I was going. Because I had really wanted to be just a jazz player and then all this explosion happened and then, whatever Miles Davis did, everybody did. If Miles got a wah-wah pedal, everybody played with a wah-wah pedal. Trumpet players, saxophone players, it didn’t matter. Of course guitar players always had the wah-wah pedal.
